raw_case_text:
A 49-year-old, nonsmoking female had been treated for AML with one course of induction chemotherapy with the use of daunorubicin and cytosine arabinoside (ARA-C). After relapse of AML, the patient was treated with 10 mg/m2 IV mitoxantrone daily for six days and 3 g/m2 IV ARA-C, daily for six days. On day six, flu-like symptoms including fever and cough developed after completion of the chemotherapy. On examination, the patient had an elevated temperature (38.5 C) and tachypnea. Chest auscultation revealed diffuse bilateral inspiratory crackles. The results of arterial blood gas analysis in room air were as follows: PaO2 92 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg and pH, 7.37. The results of a laboratory evaluation were as follows: hemoglobin level, 104 g/L; platelet count, 140,000/microL; white blood cell count, 11,100/microL. The level of C-reactive protein and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate did not increase. Chest radiograph showed mild linear and small patchy opacities in both lower lung fields. Multiple blood and sputum cultures drawn were all negative. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed patent airways and the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was non-diagnostic. Culture and microscopy of sputum and BAL materials were negative for fungi, bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, Pneumocystis carinii and cytomegalovirus. Empirical antibiotic therapy was initiated for a case of presumed pneumonia.
Over the next few days, fever and cough persisted in spite of the antibiotic treatment. On day 11, chest radiograph demonstrated a bilateral and symmetrical distribution of multiple pulmonary nodules (Fig. 1A). Twenty hours later, a chest computed tomography (CT) scan confirmed the presence of numerous discrete 1-mm to 5-mm nodules throughout the lungs (Fig. 1B, C). Due to the poor response to the antibiotic treatment and the questionable diagnosis of pulmonary metastases, a video-assisted thoracoscopic lung biopsy with wedge resection of the posterior segment of the right upper lobe was performed on day 13. Histopathological analysis revealed that polypoid granulation tissue was filling the air spaces and foamy macrophages and inflammatory cells with interstitial pneumonia and air-space fibrosis were present, consistent with COP (Fig. 1D, E). Dramatic improvement of the clinical symptoms and radiographic abnormalities was noted after two weeks of appropriate steroid treatment (Fig. 1F), and the lesions were almost completely resolved after three weeks (Fig. 1G). At a follow-up visit one month after discharge, the patient remained asymptomatic and chest radiograph showed a stable appearance.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old nonsmoking female with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia developed flu-like symptoms of fever and cough on day 6 after salvage mitoxantrone and high-dose cytarabine chemotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had previously received induction chemotherapy with daunorubicin and cytosine arabinoside (ARA-C) for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Following AML relapse, she completed a 6-day salvage regimen of intravenous mitoxantrone (10 mg/m2/day for 6 days) and high-dose ARA-C (3 g/m2/day for 6 days). On day 6 after completing chemotherapy, she developed acute flu-like symptoms including fever and cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) status post daunorubicin/ARA-C induction and mitoxantrone/high-dose ARA-C salvage chemotherapy; lifetime nonsmoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, flu-like malaise, and cough.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile with body temperature 38.5 °C and tachypneic; chest auscultation revealed diffuse bilateral inspiratory crackles.
objective.routine_investigations: Room-air arterial blood gas: pH 7.37, PaO2 92 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg. Complete blood count and inflammatory markers: Hemoglobin 104 g/L, platelets 140,000/μL, WBC 11,100/μL; normal C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Microbiology: Multiple blood and sputum cultures negative. Initial chest radiograph: Mild linear and small patchy opacities in both lower lung fields; repeat chest radiograph on day 11 showed a bilateral, symmetric distribution of multiple discrete pulmonary nodules.
objective.advanced_workup: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Patent airways; BAL fluid microscopy and cultures were negative for bacteria, fungi, acid-fast bacilli, Pneumocystis carinii, and cytomegalovirus. Chest CT (day 12): Numerous discrete 1-mm to 5-mm micronodules distributed symmetrically throughout both lungs. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) wedge biopsy of the right upper lobe posterior segment (day 13): Polypoid granulation tissue plugs filling the alveolar airspaces (Masson bodies), alveolar foamy macrophages, interstitial pneumonia, and airspace fibrosis, diagnostic of cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Nodular cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP; confirmed by VATS right upper lobe wedge biopsy histopathology) following mitoxantrone and high-dose cytarabine chemotherapy for relapsed AML; infectious etiologies including Pneumocystis carinii, fungi, mycobacteria, and CMV were excluded by negative BAL and sputum studies. Plan and clinical course: After failing initial empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, corticosteroid therapy was initiated following VATS biopsy confirmation, producing dramatic clinical and radiographic improvement within 2 weeks and near-complete resolution of pulmonary nodules after 3 weeks. She remained asymptomatic with a stable chest radiograph at 1-month post-discharge follow-up.
